quotes.t: Nothing is more to me than myself.
quotes.c: The Ego and Its Own / The Unique and Its Property (1845), Cambridge 1995, p. 7

quotes.t: The men of the future will yet fight their way to many a liberty that we do not even miss.
quotes.c: The Ego and Its Own / The Unique and Its Property (1845), Cambridge 1995, p. 114

quotes.t: Where the world comes in my way - and it comes in my way everywhere - I consume it to quiet the hunger of my egoism. For me you are nothing but - my food, even as I too am fed upon and turned to use by you. We have only one relation to each other, that of usableness, of utility, of use. We owe each other nothing, for what I seem to owe you I owe at most to myself. If I show you a cheery air in order to cheer you likewise, then your cheeriness is of consequence to me, and my air serves my wish; to a thousand others, whom I do not aim to cheer, I do not show it.
quotes.c: The Ego and Its Own / The Unique and Its Property (1845), Dover 2005, p. 296, 297

quotes.t: Whoever will be free must make himself free. Freedom is no fairy gift to fall into a man's lap. What is freedom? To have the will to be responsible for one's self.
quotes.c: Attributed in Forbes Vol 38 Iss. 2 (1936) p. 18, and in Lifetime Speaker's Encyclopedia (1962) by Jacob Morton Braude, p. 275

quotes.t: "Freedom" awakens your rage against everything that is not you; "egoism" calls you to joy over yourselves, to self-enjoyment.
quotes.c: The Ego and Its Own / The Unique and Its Property (1845), Dover 2005, p. 163

quotes.t: A people cannot be free otherwise than at the individual's expense; for it is not the individual that is the main point in this liberty, but the people. The freer the people, the more bound the individual; the Athenian people, precisely at its freest time, created ostracism, banished the atheists, poisoned the most honest thinker.
quotes.c: The Ego and Its Own / The Unique and Its Property (1845), Cambridge 1995, p. 190

quotes.t: A word of honour, an oath, is one only for him whom I entitle to receive it; he who forces me to it obtains only a forced, a hostile word, the word of a foe, whom one has no right to trust; for the foe does not give us the right.
quotes.c: The Ego and Its Own / The Unique and Its Property (1845), Cambridge 1995, p. 269

quotes.t: An appeal to men's self-sacrificing disposition and self-renouncing love ought at least to have lost its seductive plausibility when, after an activity of thousands of years, it has left nothing behind but the - misery of today. Why then still fruitlessly expect self-sacrifice to bring us better times? Why not rather hope for them from usurpation? Salvation comes no longer from the giver, the bestower, the loving one, but from the taker, the appropriator (usurper), the owner. Communism, and, consciously, egoism-reviling humanism, still count on love.
quotes.c: The Ego and Its Own / The Unique and Its Property (1845), Cambridge 1995, p. 274

quotes.t: Apart from any other basis which might justify a superiority, education, as a power, raised him who possessed it over the weak, who lacked it, and the educated man counted in his circle, however large or small it was, as the mighty, the powerful, the imposing one: for he was an authority.
quotes.c: The False Principle of our Education (1842), p. 12

quotes.t: Atheists keep up their scoffing at the higher being, which was also honoured under the name of the 'highest' or être suprême, and trample in the dust one 'proof of his existence' after another, without noticing that they themselves, out of need for a higher being, only annihilate the old to make room for a new.
quotes.c: The Ego and Its Own / The Unique and Its Property (1845), Cambridge 1995, p. 38-39

quotes.t: Because the Egoist is to himself the warder of the human, and has nothing to say to the state except: "Get out of my sunshine!"
quotes.c: The Ego and Its Own / The Unique and Its Property (1845), Tucker 1907, p. 307

quotes.t: Do I write out of love to men? No, I write because I want to procure for my thoughts an existence in the world; and, even if I foresaw that these thoughts would deprive you of your rest and your peace, even if I saw the bloodiest wars and the fall of many generations springing up from this seed of thought - I would nevertheless scatter it. Do with it what you will and can, that is your affair and does not trouble me.
quotes.c: The Ego and Its Own / The Unique and Its Property (1845), Cambridge 1995, p. 262, 263

quotes.t: Egoism, as Stirner uses it, is not opposed to love nor to thought; it is no enemy of the sweet life of love, nor of devotion and sacrifice; it is no enemy of intimate warmth, but it is also no enemy of critique, nor of socialism, nor, in short, of any actual interest. It doesn't exclude any interest. It is directed against only disinterestedness and the uninteresting; not against love, but against sacred love, not against thought, but against sacred thought, not against socialists, but against sacred socialists, etc.
quotes.c: Stirner's Critics (1845), Landstreicher, 20

quotes.t: Every love to which there clings but the smallest speck of obligation is an unselfish love, and, so far as this speck reaches, a possessedness. He who believes that he owes the object of his love anything loves romantically or religiously.
quotes.c: The Ego and Its Own / The Unique and Its Property (1845), Cambridge 1995, p. 260

quotes.t: Everything sacred is a tie, a fetter.
quotes.c: The Ego and Its Own / The Unique and Its Property (1845), Cambridge 1995, p. 192

quotes.t: Feuerbach... recognizes... "even love, in itself the truest, most inward sentiment, becomes an obscure, illusory one through religiousness, since religious love loves man only for God's sake, therefore loves man only apparently, but in truth God only." Is this different with moral love? Does it love the man, this man for this man's sake, or for morality's sake, for Man's sake, and so-for homo homini Deus-for God's sake?
quotes.c: The Ego and Its Own / The Unique and Its Property (1845), Cambridge 1995, p. 56

quotes.t: For the state it is indispensable that nobody have an own will; if one had, the state would have to exclude (lock up, banish, etc.) this one; if all had, they would do away with the state. (...) The own will of me is the state's destroyer; it is therefore denounced by the state as 'self-will'. Own will and the state are powers in deadly hostility, between which no 'perpetual peace' is possible. As long as the state asserts itself, it represents own will, its ever-hostile opponent, as unreasonable, evil; and the latter lets itself be talked into believing this.
quotes.c: The Ego and Its Own / The Unique and Its Property (1845), Cambridge 1995, p. 174, 175

quotes.t: He who is infatuated with Man leaves persons out of account so far as that infatuation extends, and floats in an ideal, sacred interest. Man, you see, is not a person, but an ideal, a spook.
quotes.c: The Ego and Its Own / The Unique and Its Property (1845), Dover 2005, p. 79

quotes.t: History seeks for man: but he is I, you, we. Sought as a mysterious essence, as the divine, first as God, then as man (humanity, humaneness, and mankind), he is found as the individual, the finite, the unique one.
quotes.c: The Ego and Its Own / The Unique and Its Property (1845), Cambridge 1995, p. 217

quotes.t: Human or general needs can be satisfied through society; for satisfaction of unique needs you must do some seeking. A friend and a friendly service, or even an individual's service, society cannot procure you. And yet you will every moment be in need of such a service, and on the slightest occasions require somebody who is helpful to you. Therefore do not rely on society, but see to it that you have the wherewithal to - purchase the fulfilment of your wishes.
quotes.c: The Ego and Its Own / The Unique and Its Property (1845), Cambridge 1995, p. 243

quotes.t: I am owner of my might, and I am so when I know myself as unique. In the unique one the owner himself returns into his creative nothing, of which he is born. Every higher essence above me, be it God, be it man, weakens the feeling of my uniqueness, and pales only before the sun of this consciousness. If I concern myself for myself, the unique one, then my concern rests on its transitory, mortal creator, who consumes himself, and I may say: All things are nothing to me.
quotes.c: The Ego and Its Own / The Unique and Its Property (1845), Dover 2005, p. 366

quotes.t: I have no need to take up each thing that wants to throw its cause on us and show that it is occupied only with itself, not with us, only with its good, not with ours. Look at the rest for yourselves. Do truth, freedom, humanity, justice, desire anything else than that you grow enthusiastic and serve them?
quotes.c: The Ego and Its Own / The Unique and Its Property (1845), Cambridge 1995, p. 6

quotes.t: I love men too, not merely individuals, but every one. But I love them with the consciousness of egoism; I love them because love makes me happy, I love because loving is natural to me, because it pleases me. I know no 'commandment of love'.
quotes.c: The Ego and Its Own / The Unique and Its Property (1845), Cambridge 1995, p. 258

quotes.t: Ich setze Mich nicht voraus, weil Ich Mich jeden Augenblick überhaupt erst setze oder schaffe, und nur dadurch Ich bin, dass Ich nicht vorausgesetzt, sondern gesetzt bin, und wiederum nur in dem Moment gesetzt, wo ich mich setze, d.h. Ich bin Schöpfer un Geschöpf in Einem.
quotes.c: The Ego and Its Own / The Unique and Its Property (1845), I do not presuppose myself, because I am every moment just positing or creating myself, and am I only by being not presupposed but posited, and... only in the moment when I posit myself; that is, I am creator and creature in one. Cambridge 1995, p. 135

quotes.t: If a concept lacks an essence, nothing will ever be found that completely fits that concept. If you are lacking in the concept of human being, it will immediately expose that you are something individual, something that cannot be expressed by the term human being, thus, in every instance, an individual human being.
quotes.c: Stirner's Critics (1845), Landstreicher, p. 16

quotes.t: If man puts his honor first in relying upon himself, knowing himself and applying himself, this in self-reliance, self-assertion, and freedom, he then strives to rid himself of the ignorance which makes a strange impenetrable object a barrier and a hindrance to his self-knowledge.
quotes.c: The False Principle of our Education (1842), p. 23

quotes.t: If one awakens in men the idea of freedom then the free men will incessantly go on to free themselves; if on the contrary, one only educates them, then they will at all times accommodate themselves to circumstance in the most highly educated and elegant manner and degenerate into subservient cringing souls.
quotes.c: The False Principle of our Education (1842), p. 23

quotes.t: If religion has put forward the proposition that we are all of us sinners, I set another against it: we are all of us perfect! Because, in each moment, we are all we can be, and never need to be more.
quotes.c: The Ego and Its Own / The Unique and Its Property (1845), Landstreicher, p. 226

quotes.t: If the church had deadly sins, the state has capital crimes; if the one had heretics, the other has traitors; the one ecclesiastical penalties, the other criminal penalties; the one inquisitorial processes, the other fiscal; in short, there sins, here crimes, there inquisition and here - inquisition. Will the sanctity of the state not fall like the church's? The awe of its laws, the reverence for its highness, the humility of its 'subjects', will this remain? Will the 'saint's' face not be stripped of its adornment?
quotes.c: The Ego and Its Own / The Unique and Its Property (1845), Cambridge 1995, p. 211, 212

quotes.t: If the press was to be free, nothing would be so important as precisely its liberation from every coercion that could be put on it in the name of a law. And, that it might come to that, I my own self should have to have absolved myself from obedience to the law.
quotes.c: The Ego and Its Own / The Unique and Its Property (1845), Cambridge 1995, p. 249

quotes.t: In the pedagogical as in certain other spheres freedom is not allowed to erupt, the power of the opposition is not allowed to put a word in edgewise: they want submissiveness. Only a formal and material training is being aimed at and only scholars come out of the menageries of the humanists, only "useful citizens" out of those of the realists, both of whom are indeed nothing but subservient people. Our good background of recalcitrancy gets strongly suppressed and with it the development of knowledge to free will. The result of school is then philistinism.
quotes.c: The False Principle of our Education (1842), p. 23

quotes.t: It is truly not the merit of the school if we do not come out selfish. Each sort of corresponding pride and every wind of covetousness, eagerness for office, mechanical and servile officiousness, hypocrisy, etc., is bound as much with extensive knowledge as with elegant, classical education, and since this whole instruction exercises no influence of any sort on our ethical behavior, it thus frequently falls to the fate of being forgotten in the same measure as it is not used: one shakes off the dust of the school.
quotes.c: The False Principle of our Education (1842), p. 22

quotes.t: It would be foolish to assert that there is no power above mine. Only the attitude that I take toward it will be quite another than that of the religious age: I shall be the enemy of every higher power, while religion teaches us to make it our friend and be humble toward it.
quotes.c: The Ego and Its Own / The Unique and Its Property (1845), Dover 2005, p. 184

quotes.t: Liberty of the people is not my liberty!
quotes.c: The Ego and Its Own / The Unique and Its Property (1845), Cambridge 1995, p. 190 The freer the people, the more bound the individual.

quotes.t: Look upon yourself as more powerful than they give you out for, and you have more power; look upon yourself as more, and you have more.
quotes.c: The Ego and Its Own / The Unique and Its Property (1845), Cambridge 1995, p. 318

quotes.t: Man with the great M is only an ideal, the species only something thought of.
quotes.c: The Ego and Its Own / The Unique and Its Property (1845), Dover 2005, p. 182

quotes.t: Might is a fine thing, and useful for many purposes; for 'one goes further with a handful of might than with a bagful of right'. You long for freedom? You fools! If you took might, freedom would come of itself. See, he who has might 'stands above the law'. How does this prospect taste to you, you 'law-abiding' people? But you have no taste!
quotes.c: The Ego and Its Own / The Unique and Its Property (1845), Cambridge 1995, p. 151

quotes.t: Now why, if freedom is striven after for love of the I after all - why not choose the I himself as beginning, middle, and end?
quotes.c: The Ego and Its Own / The Unique and Its Property (1845), Dover 2005, p. 163

quotes.t: Now, on the contrary, when every one is to cultivate himself into man, condemning a man to machine-like labor amounts to the same thing as slavery. If a factory-worker must tire himself to death twelve hours and more, he is cut off from becoming man. Every labor is to have the intent that the man be satisfied. His labor is nothing taken by itself, has no object in itself, is nothing complete in itself; he labors only into another's hands, and is used (exploited) by this other.
quotes.c: The Ego and Its Own / The Unique and Its Property (1845), Cambridge 1995, p. 108

quotes.t: On the contrary, to educate rational people, that should be sufficient; it is not really intended for sensible people; to understand things and conditions, there is the matter ended,-to understand oneself does not seem to be everyman's concern.
quotes.c: The False Principle of our Education (1842), p. 22

quotes.t: One is not worthy to have what one, through weakness, lets be taken from him; one is not worthy of it because one is not capable of it.
quotes.c: The Ego and Its Own / The Unique and Its Property (1845)

quotes.t: People is the name of the body, State of the spirit, of that ruling person that has hitherto suppressed me.
quotes.c: The Ego and Its Own / The Unique and Its Property (1845), Dover 2005, p. 242

quotes.t: Political freedom means this: that the polis, the state, is free; religious freedom this: that religion is free, just as freedom of conscience indicates that conscience is free; thus, it does not that I am free from state, from religion, from conscience, or that I am rid of them. It does not mean my freedom, but the freedom of a power that rules and vanquishes me; it means that one of my oppressors, like state, religion, conscience, is free.
quotes.c: The Ego and Its Own / The Unique and Its Property (1845), Landstreicher, p. 76

quotes.t: Revolution is aimed at new arrangements; insurrection leads us no longer to let ourselves be arranged, but to arrange ourselves, and set no glittering hopes on "institutions."
quotes.c: The Ego and Its Own / The Unique and Its Property (1845), S. Byington, trans. (1913), p. 421

quotes.t: The State's behavior is violence, and it calls its violence "law"; that of the individual, "crime."
quotes.c: The Ego and Its Own / The Unique and Its Property (1845), The state calls its own violence law, but that of the individual, crime. As quoted in The Great Quotations (1960) by George Seldes, p. 664

quotes.t: The difficulty in our education up till now lies, for the most part, in the fact that knowledge did not refine itself into will, to application of itself, to pure practice. The realists felt the need and supplied it, though in a most miserable way, by cultivating idea-less and fettered "practical men." Most college students are living examples of this sad turn of events. Trained in the most excellent manner, they go on training; drilled they continue drilling.
quotes.c: The False Principle of our Education (1842), p. 25

quotes.t: The divine is God's concern; the human, man's. My concern is neither the divine nor the human, not the true, good, just, free, etc., but solely what is mine, and it is not a general one, but is - unique, as I am unique. Nothing is more to me than myself!
quotes.c: The Ego and Its Own / The Unique and Its Property (1845), Cambridge 1995, p. 7

quotes.t: The habit of the religious way of thinking has biased our mind so grievously that we are - terrified at ourselves in our nakedness and naturalness; it has degraded us so that we deem ourselves depraved by nature, born devils.
quotes.c: The Ego and Its Own / The Unique and Its Property (1845), Dover 2005, p. 162

quotes.t: The republic is nothing whatever but - absolute monarchy; for it makes no difference whether the monarch is called prince or people, both being a 'majesty'.
quotes.c: The Ego and Its Own / The Unique and Its Property (1845), Cambridge 1995, p. 202, 203

quotes.t: The tiger that assails me is in the right, and I who strike him down am also in the right. I defend against him not my right, but myself.
quotes.c: The Ego and Its Own / The Unique and Its Property (1845), S. Byington, trans. (1913), p. 191

quotes.t: The will is not fundamentally right, as the practical ones would like very much to assure us; one may not pass over the desire for knowledge in order to stand immediately in the will, but knowledge perfects itself to will when it desensualizes itself and creates itself as a spirit "which builds its own body."
quotes.c: The False Principle of our Education (1842), p. 21

quotes.t: The workers have the most enormous power in their hands, and if one day they became truly aware of it and used it, then nothing could resist them; they would only have to stop work and look upon the products of work as their own and enjoy them. This is the meaning of the labor unrest that is looming here and there. The state is founded on the-slavery of labor. If labor becomes free, the state is lost.
quotes.c: The Ego and Its Own / The Unique and Its Property (1845), Landstreicher 2017, p. 133

quotes.t: The young are of age when they twitter like the old; they are driven through school to learn the old song, and, when they have this by heart, they are declared of age.
quotes.c: The Ego and Its Own / The Unique and Its Property (1845), Cambridge 1995, pp. 61-62

quotes.t: Thus the radii of all education run together into one center which is called personality.
quotes.c: The False Principle of our Education (1842), p. 25

quotes.t: What is not supposed to be my concern! First and foremost, the Good Cause, then God's cause, the cause of mankind, of truth, of freedom, of humanity, of justice; further, the cause of my people, my prince, my fatherland; finally, even the cause of Mind, and a thousand other causes. Only my cause is never to be my concern. "Shame on the egoist who thinks only of himself!"
quotes.c: The Ego and Its Own / The Unique and Its Property (1845), Cambridge 1995, p. 5

quotes.t: What matters the party to me? I shall find enough anyhow who unite with me without swearing allegiance to my flag.
quotes.c: The Ego and Its Own / The Unique and Its Property (1845), Dover 2005, p. 236

quotes.t: Whoso is full of sacred (religious, moral, humane) love loves only the spook, the "true man," and persecutes with dull mercilessness the individual, the real man.
quotes.c: The Ego and Its Own / The Unique and Its Property (1845), S. Byington, trans. (1913), p. 383

quotes.t: Wollen wir etwa die Pädagogik den Philosophen in die Hände spielen? Nichts weniger als das! Sie würden sich ungeschickt genug benehmen. Denen allein werde sie anvertraut, die mehr sind als Philosophen, darum aber auch unendlich mehr als Humanisten oder Realisten.
quotes.c: The False Principle of our Education (1842), Do we want to put pedagogy into the hands of the philosophers? Nothing less than that! They would behave themselves awkwardly enough. It shall be entrusted only to those who are more than philosophers, who are in that respect more even than humanists or realists. p. 19

quotes.t: Yes, so it is that knowledge itself must die in order to blossom forth again in death as will; the freedom of thought, belief, and conscience, these wonderful flowers of three centuries will sink back into the lap of mother earth so that a new freedom, the freedom will, will be nourished with its most noble juices.
quotes.c: The False Principle of our Education (1842), p. 19

quotes.t: then the necessary decline of non-voluntary learning and rise of the self-assured will which perfects itself in the glorious sunlight of the free person may be somewhat expressed as follows: knowledge must die and rise again as will and create itself anew each day as a free person.
quotes.c: The False Principle of our Education (1842), p. 28

quotes.t: I am every moment putting off from me my state, my calling, my talent, my virtue, my spirit, but I cannot put off myself.
I am my own purpose, and I am not the means to any purpose which is not my own.
I am nobody's means to an end.
I am not a believer in any dogma, but my own beliefs.
I am not a citizen of any state, but a citizen of the world.
I am not a dream in any dreamer, but a dreamer in myself.
I am not a follower of any leader, but my own leader.
I am not a means to an end, but an end in myself.
I am not a member of any church, but a free spirit.
I am not a moral being, but a natural one.
I am not a note in any symphony, but a symphony in myself.
I am not a part of any whole, but a whole in myself.
I am not a reflection in any mirror, but a mirror in myself.
I am not a servant of any cause, but my own cause.
I am not a slave to any master, but my own master.
I am not a subject of any authority, but my own authority.
I am not a thought in any mind, but a mind in myself.
I am not a tool for any purpose, but my own purpose.
I am not a word in any language, but a language in myself.
I am nothing in the world but my own self, and I must fulfill myself according to my nature.
I am the absolute, the infinite, the eternal.
I am the annihilation of all that is not myself.
I am the beginning and the end of all things.
I am the consumption of all that is not myself.
I am the creator of the world, for it is my world.
I am the destruction of all that is not myself.
I am the devouring of all that is not myself.
I am the dissolution of all that is not myself.
I am the foundation of all being.
I am the measure of all things.
I am the negation of all that is not myself.
I am the only reality, all else is mere appearance.
I am the self-affirmation of the world.
I am the self-assertion of all that is not myself.
I do not set up the least-moral worldly principle against the highest-moral one, but I declare war against the principle of morality itself.
I have no other merit and no other aim than being I, than asserting myself.
The only law that I recognize is that of my own nature.
The only truth is that I am.
The unique one is unique precisely because of his nothingness.
